Earlier this week, a sentinel reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery. The incident followed a wreath-laying ceremony marking Veterans Day.

The Pentagon have since announced that Hegseth has given the soldier, Specialist Thomas Iglesias, a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier".

BBC's Bernd Debusmann breaks down why Hegseth's group was reprimanded, the history behind the strict rules governing visitor behaviour and the importance of maintaining an atmosphere of silence at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

Radio 5 Live , · 12 Nov 2026 , · 32 mins

Reaction from Wembley as Harry Kane becomes the most-capped England men's player in history. England beat Croatia 2-1 to confirm their place in the Nations League quarter finals but it was Harry Kane's night as he scored in his 126th appearance. Kelly Somers is joined by former England goalkeepers Paul Robinson and Rob Green, as well as correspondent John Murray and senior football reporter Ian Dennis. Morgan Rogers tells us that Cole Palmer wants to be playing for England and that any suggestions otherwise are "nonsense." Plus, hear from the England manager Thomas Tuchel, who looks ahead to Sunday's game against Spain. Timecodes: 2'30 Kane's night 15'38 Harry Kane interview 21'30 Morgan Rogers interview 26'41 Thomas Tuchel interview

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee about his alleged affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang abruptly quit on Thursday as head of one of the world's most valuable companies after revelations of alleged extramarital affairs, in a stunning fall from grace that sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is under scrutiny over exports of sensitive Nvidia AI chips to China, has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December.

Nvidia has lost $550bn (£415bn) in stock market value in just five days as the scandal dominated headlines.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters on Thursday to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," the South Carolina Republican posted on X.

"The American people deserve answers," he added.

Scott asked Huang to appear voluntarily on 3 December, but also warned the panel could issue a subpoena to compel his testimony.

Three House of Representatives committees - on intelligence and foreign affairs and a panel on China - have also sent a letter to Huang summoning him for a closed-door interview on 1 December.

How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions

Lutnick is under scrutiny because unnamed officials in President Donald Trump's administration have been briefing US media that the commerce secretary stalled efforts to tighten export restrictions on advanced AI chips to China.

A commerce department spokesperson told US media that Lutnick had "proactively" agreed to appear before the Senate Banking Committee.

Huang, who has been Nvidia's public face since 1993, admitted on Sunday to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

On Wednesday, he was reported to have had a second relationship, this time with an Nvidia executive.

Alice Huang (no relation) worked as an executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. She has been suspected of being an intelligence asset for China, according to the New York Times. China has rejected that allegation as a smear.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also been summoned to appear before the Senate Banking Committee in December

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Department of Justice had not yet drawn any conclusions about whether Alice Huang was engaged in espionage for Beijing.

Nvidia officials have repeatedly declined to comment since Wednesday. A personal representative of Huang also declined to comment on Thursday.

According to US media, Huang's alleged second affair was with a long-time Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reported directly to him within the company.

Sources have told the BBC that Nvidia employees had noticed the pair were unusually close.

Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Huang had been widely expected to weather the storm after the first affair became public, even as Nvidia announced it had launched an investigation into whether its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

One current Nvidia staff member told the BBC that the initial reports of his infidelity were more or less brushed off by rank-and-file workers inside the company.

It wasn't until Huang's alleged affair with the Nvidia executive became public that workers started to feel "this is crazy", the person said.

Another Nvidia employee said they had been told not to speak with the press or otherwise comment on the situation in public.

Many staff have earned millions of dollars in compensation through their ability to cash out their Nvidia shares as the stock soared.

Nvidia has said it has "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised", but pledged that its independent inquiry would look at all available information.

The company's meteoric rise had been led by Jensen Huang, who became a major booster of the AI industry, which relies on Nvidia for the powerful computer chips it manufactures.

Initially those chips were designed for computer gaming.

But as AI technology evolved in the last four years into chatbots and large language models, companies building AI tools suddenly required huge numbers of the Nvidia computer chips that could process large amounts of data.

Nvidia is now hunting a permanent replacement for Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named on Thursday as interim CEO.

Several tech insiders that the BBC spoke with this week noted that Huang's downfall has been a major topic of conversation in San Francisco Bay area circles, an area filled with tech employees, industry executives and billionaires.

Huang has been married to Lori Huang for 40 years. Both of their children are also executives at Nvidia.

Nvidia's stock fall this week is the most significant five-day drop the company has seen since going public 27 years ago.

Its market value rose by more than 470% in the past five years, peaking just a few weeks ago. It is now down by 31% against a backdrop of wider uncertainty in the tech sector.

Jensen Huang has resigned, what's next for Nvidia?

Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair

Donald Danforth Plant Science Center, the world’s largest independent nonprofit research institute dedicated to plant science is building partnership with the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA).

The development is taking shape from an already existing partnership with the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resource Development Board (RAB) in combating Cassava Brown Streak Disease, a major constraint to cassava production in Rwanda.

The Danforth Center intends to expand its engagement from cassava disease research into broader crop improvement, conservation agriculture and scientific workforce development.

“Well, so far, it’s really been focused on Brown Streak Disease in cassava. And so, the field trials that are going on right now, which has really solved that problem,” said Dr. Giles Oldroyd, President of Donald Danforth Plant Science Centre.

Dr. Giles Oldroyd, President of Donald Danforth Plant Science Centre

From the Headquarters of Donald Danforth Plant Science Center in Saint Louis – Missouri, Dr. Giles was accompanied by a delegation of his County, including the Mayor, yesterday.

“Looking forward,” he said, “I see huge opportunities for working here at RICA on developing conservation agriculture, expanding the focus outside of cassava to also include other crops like maize and sorghum, millets. These are all crops that we work on, as well as beans. That’s a crop that I’m excited to start working on.”

“I see an opportunity to really expand the collaboration, both with RAB and with RICA, and as part of the broader Rwandan Food Innovation Partnership.”

The Food Innovation Partnership was initiated by the Government of Rwanda to turn Rwanda into a hub for food systems innovation. RICA is a key partner and founding member of the program.

Narrowing down on the partnership with RICA for example, Dr. Giles said that his institution sees an opportunity for much more exchange with students from Rwanda and the US reciprocating field visits.

For Dr. Giles, joining the partnership and particularly seeing the opportunities offered by RICA, he said “I could see a really fantastic opportunity of expanding the work we do in sustainability and conservation agriculture to also include crops that are relevant here.”

“I think what we bring to that discussion on conservation agriculture is crop improvement,” Dr. Giles said.

A partnership built on complementary strengths

For Dr. Momar Dieng, Vice Chancellor of the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture (RICA), the emerging collaboration with the Donald Danforth Plant Science Center presents an opportunity to bring together two institutions with complementary expertise and a shared commitment to agricultural innovation.

The Danforth Center, based in St. Louis, Missouri, is internationally recognized for its research in plant science and crop improvement. RICA, meanwhile, combines agricultural education, practical research, and field-based training, with a particular focus on farming methods that improve productivity while preserving soil health and natural resources.

“What makes this partnership particularly promising is the opportunity to connect world-class scientific research with practical agricultural challenges here in Rwanda. Both institutions have expertise and capabilities that can benefit the other,” Dr. Dieng explained.

One area of potential collaboration involves developing crop varieties that are not only more productive and resistant to diseases, but also better suited to sustainable farming practices.

The guest delegation was given tour of the Institute’s demo sites

Researchers at the Danforth Center are exploring how improvements in crop varieties can complement conservation agriculture, including farming methods that protect the soil, make better use of water, and reduce dependence on chemical inputs. RICA’s fields and research facilities could provide opportunities to study how these approaches perform under local growing conditions.

Another promising area is the use of advanced imaging technologies, data analysis, and artificial intelligence to monitor crop development and understand how different varieties respond to soil conditions, farming practices, and environmental stresses.

For RICA, such collaboration could strengthen applied research while creating new opportunities for students, graduates, and faculty to participate in scientific projects addressing challenges facing African agriculture.

Dr. Dieng also emphasized the value of RICA’s distinctive educational model, which places practical experience at the heart of learning.

“Our students learn by doing. They work directly with crops, livestock, equipment, and agricultural technologies, gaining the practical experience needed to translate scientific knowledge into solutions for farmers and agribusinesses,” he said.

He noted that this combination of education, research, and practical application makes RICA a potentially valuable partner for international research institutions seeking to test and adapt innovations to African farming conditions.

“Ultimately, the measure of success will be whether we can turn scientific discoveries into better farming practices, stronger agricultural systems, and improved livelihoods for farmers,” Dr. Dieng concluded.

Cole Palmer and Morgan are Chelsea team-mates

Morgan Rogers says any suggestion Cole Palmer is not committed to England "is a lie" and "nonsense".

Rogers scored the opener in Wednesday's 2-1 Uefa Nations League win over Croatia , with Harry Kane adding a penalty on his record-breaking 126th appearance for the men's side.

But his Chelsea team-mate, and childhood friend, Palmer had been left out of the squad after boss Thomas Tuchel said he "misses too many chances to impress".

The 24-year-old Palmer, who was also not called up for the World Cup, withdrew from the previous England camp in September citing a minor injury.

Forward Rogers, also 24, was asked about the criticism of Palmer following the win at Wembley, and told BBC Radio 5 Live: "He wants to be here.

"He wanted to get called up and he wanted to come and represent his country as he always has done.

"He was in quite a low place with his injuries last year and didn't feel 100% himself on the pitch, so he wants to be here and he wants to be the best version of himself.

"But he also has to look at his body. He wants to play for 10 or 15 years, he also has to manage himself. If he has to manage himself in the short term for the greater good then he has to do that and you have to fully support it.

"It has nothing to do with England or not wanting to play with England. It's a nonsense really that people are questioning someone that wants to play for England. It's a lie.

"You see the joy and smile on his face, how much he loves the game, so I honestly don't get it and he doesn't get it."

Is Palmer's England career over under Tuchel?

A must pick or unreliable? Tuchel's Palmer dilemma

History for Kane but what would England do without him?

In the three years since his England debut, Palmer has only won 14 caps, scoring two goals - including one in the Euro 2024 final defeat by Spain - and having one assist.

That is despite scoring 50 Premier League goals with 24 assists.

He was named England's men's player of the year for the 2023-24 season after some impressive form, including his strike against Spain in the Berlin showpiece.

But Palmer has only featured in three of Tuchel's 27 games since he succeeded Gareth Southgate as manager.

Some sketchy form last season, though, meant the former Manchester City player missed out on the the summer World Cup, with England going on to finish third after losing to Argentina in the semi-final.

He was named in Tuchel's first squad after that, but withdrew despite having played in all Chelsea's league games to that point.

Tuchel said this week: "We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception.

"We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."

But the German added: "It's not personal. We will never assume Cole is in the mindset never to come to the camp.

"Cole is always in our mindset but the competition is on."

Record-breaker Kane scores winner as England qualify for quarters

Kane's top 10 England moments - which was your favourite?

Palmer should not give up hope of getting back into Tuchel's good books.

Last October, Jude Bellingham was left out of the squad for a friendly against Wales and a World Cup qualifier against Latvia.

The Real Madrid midfielder then ended up being a key part of the England team at the World Cup, scoring seven goals.

Former Three Lions goalkeeper Paul Robinson added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "You can see what Tuchel is doing when you look at what he's done with Jude Bellingham.

"It was only 12 months or so that Bellingham was getting left out of an England squad. Call it what you want, but it was management from Tuchel to make Bellingham realise that he wasn't the lone star of this team - the team was the star.

"The team was better with Bellingham in it, playing at his highest level.

"There was a lesson in his management skills with Bellingham and I wouldn't be surprised if he's doing the same now."

Where does Kane rank among all-time England greats?

Quiz: Name England men's all-time leading appearance makers

MN202611_1ihdok96l13.t:
Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago

When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.

Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales in November 2025 .

But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.

"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."

The BBC report from last year when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia

Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of 15 November as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.

It has officially been described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in the Welsh town during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.

Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.

"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend most days who was staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms.

"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."

Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth, and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end

"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."

Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.

Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.

"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.

This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia

"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."

The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events .

Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter, with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable" .

Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia

Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.

"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.

"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."

Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.

Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia

One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.

The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surged towards her end-of-terrace cottage.

"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.

"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."

What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.

This was what Emily Frost saw of her house, on the left of this picture, as she looked back while their family were evacuated on a life raft during Monmouth's flooding in November 2025

Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.

"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.

"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.

"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."

The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.

Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.

This was Emily Frost's kitchen the day after her family home was flooded for the second time in five years

"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things," said Emily.

"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."

Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.

An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.

Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.

Alan and Jennifer Morgan said they spent their life savings renovating the house Alan grew up in and has been in his family for three generations so "it means a lot to us"

"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70.

"The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer.

"People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof."

The River Monnow burst its banks and the official report into the flood said floodwater reached depths 1.5m high, almost 2.5m in some extreme cases

The official Section 19 report , external into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit.

Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening.

The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached, and after shops and homes had been flooded.

Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service , external but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated.

Prince William was in the Monmouth area in October, visiting communities affected by the 2025 flooding caused by extreme weather conditions and met with Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council

"When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said.

"Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change."

The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively".

It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow.

NRW said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons".

Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.

This is how the River Monnow usually looks at Monmouth but it swelled to 18-times its normal depth in November 2025, after torrential downpours during Storm Claudia

NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.

The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences were fit for purpose.

"We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW.

"We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact."

The Welsh government said it was spending almost £1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including £700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith.

"We have made £85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement.

NRW said they had done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they have more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains.

Storm Claudia devastated the residents of Monmouth in November 2025 when the historic market town was hit by the worst floods in living memory

"We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council.

"If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains."

Insurance companies in the UK paid out £565m to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary , external .

"I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not.

"But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."
